title: Internal Control Fault
shortDescription: Coleman furnace control board has detected an internal fault and locked out.
fullDescription:
A single LED flash on a Coleman gas furnace indicates the integrated control module has failed an internal self-check. The board cannot reliably operate the gas valve, inducer, or blower and has shut down for safety.

Most commonly this is caused by a power surge, low/high incoming voltage, or a failed control board after years of service. Less commonly it is a wiring fault that has shorted a sensor input.
safetyWarning: Do not bypass the control board. Coleman furnaces use integrated safety logic for the gas valve, flame sensor, and pressure switch. Bypassing creates a serious risk of CO poisoning, fire, or explosion.

fixSteps.title: Power cycle the furnace
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off the furnace at the service switch for 60 seconds, then restore power and watch for code to clear.

fixSteps.title: Inspect thermostat wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Open the blower compartment and check for pinched, frayed, or shorted low-voltage wires at the control board.

fixSteps.title: Replace control board
fixSteps.instruction: If code returns after a power cycle, the integrated control module typically must be replaced. Match the OEM Coleman part number exactly.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if voltage at the board is out of spec or if you are not comfortable handling 24V and 120V wiring.

faq.q: Can I reset a Coleman 1-flash code?
faq.a: A single power cycle may clear it temporarily, but if the board is failing the code will return.

faq.q: How long do Coleman control boards last?
faq.a: Typically 12-18 years. After that, a 1-flash fault often signals end-of-life.

title: Pressure Switch Stuck Closed
shortDescription: The pressure switch is closed when it should be open before the inducer starts.
fullDescription:
Two LED flashes on a Coleman furnace mean the control board is reading the pressure switch as closed before the inducer motor has started. The switch must be open at rest and only close once the inducer creates enough vacuum.

This usually points to a stuck or welded pressure switch, but it can also be caused by a wiring short between the switch terminals.
safetyWarning: A stuck-closed pressure switch defeats a critical combustion safety. Do not jumper or bypass it.

fixSteps.title: Disconnect pressure switch
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, unplug the pressure switch and use a multimeter to confirm continuity is OPEN at rest.

fixSteps.title: Replace pressure switch
fixSteps.instruction: If continuity reads closed at rest, replace with the OEM-matched pressure switch (correct WC rating).

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if the switch tests good — the issue may be a damaged board trace.

faq.q: Can debris cause a stuck pressure switch?
faq.a: Yes, water or soot in the hose or port can hold the diaphragm closed.

title: Pressure Switch Open / Inducer Failure
shortDescription: Pressure switch will not close after the inducer is energized.
fullDescription:
Three flashes indicate the inducer started but the pressure switch did not close within the trial-for-ignition window. Either the inducer is not pulling enough draft or the switch/hose path is blocked.

Common causes are blocked vent termination (snow, ice, bird nest), cracked or kinked vacuum hose, weak inducer motor, and a blocked condensate drain on high-efficiency models.
safetyWarning: Never operate a furnace with a blocked vent. Carbon monoxide can spill into the home.
symptoms: Inducer runs but ignition never starts

fixSteps.title: Inspect vent terminations
fixSteps.instruction: Go outside and clear snow, leaves, or nests from the PVC intake and exhaust pipes.

fixSteps.title: Clear condensate trap
fixSteps.instruction: Remove the trap, flush with warm water, and check the drain line for blockage.

fixSteps.title: Test pressure switch hose
fixSteps.instruction: Check the silicone hose for cracks, kinks, or moisture. Replace if suspect.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro for inducer replacement or if draft pressure tests below spec.

faq.q: Why does this code happen mostly in winter?
faq.a: Vent terminations clog with ice and snow more often in cold weather.

title: Limit Switch Open
shortDescription: High-limit safety switch has opened due to overheating.
fullDescription:
Four flashes mean the high-limit switch has tripped because the heat exchanger or plenum exceeded safe temperature. The most common reason is restricted airflow, not a bad switch.

Check the air filter first — a clogged filter is the leading cause. Other restrictions include closed supply registers, undersized ductwork, dirty blower wheel, or a failing blower motor capacitor.
safetyWarning: Repeated limit trips can crack the heat exchanger and cause CO leaks. Do not jumper the limit switch.

fixSteps.title: Replace air filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install a clean filter of the correct MERV rating. Avoid MERV 13+ on older systems.

fixSteps.title: Open all supply registers
fixSteps.instruction: Walk through the home and ensure no more than 20% of supply registers are closed.

fixSteps.title: Inspect blower wheel
fixSteps.instruction: Pull the blower assembly and clean accumulated dust from the wheel blades.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if the limit trips with a clean filter and open registers — heat exchanger inspection is needed.

faq.q: How often should I change the filter?
faq.a: Every 1-3 months depending on filter thickness and household conditions.

title: Flame Sensed With No Call for Heat
shortDescription: The flame sensor detects flame even though gas valve is off.
fullDescription:
Five flashes indicate flame is being sensed when there should be none. This is a serious safety condition because it usually means the gas valve is leaking by, or there is induced electrical noise on the flame sense circuit.

More rarely, a hot surface igniter cracking or shorting against the burner can mimic flame. Either way the furnace will lock out until corrected.
safetyWarning: A leaking gas valve is dangerous. Shut off gas at the supply if you smell gas and call a professional immediately.

fixSteps.title: Shut off gas supply
fixSteps.instruction: If you smell gas, immediately close the manual gas valve and ventilate.

fixSteps.title: Inspect flame sensor wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for chafing or shorts to ground on the flame sensor lead.

fixSteps.title: Call professional
fixSteps.instruction: If wiring looks good, the gas valve or board needs professional diagnosis.

whenToCallPro: Always call a pro for a 5-flash code — gas valve diagnosis requires manometer testing.

faq.a: Yes, it can indicate a gas leak. Shut off gas and call a pro.

title: 115V Polarity Reversed
shortDescription: Line and neutral are swapped at the furnace power feed.
fullDescription:
Six flashes mean the furnace control board detects reversed polarity on the incoming 120V supply. Modern furnaces require correct hot/neutral orientation for the flame sense circuit to reference ground properly.

This often appears after electrical work, an outlet replacement, or a new whip installation.
safetyWarning: Reversed polarity is an electrical hazard. Have a qualified electrician verify and correct.

fixSteps.title: Test outlet polarity
fixSteps.instruction: Use an outlet tester or multimeter at the furnace receptacle to verify hot/neutral.

fixSteps.title: Correct wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Have an electrician swap hot and neutral at the source.

whenToCallPro: Always use a licensed electrician for line-voltage corrections.

faq.a: Only if you are qualified to work in a panel or junction box; otherwise call an electrician.

title: Gas Valve Circuit Error
shortDescription: Control board cannot energize or de-energize the gas valve correctly.
fullDescription:
Seven flashes signal a fault on the gas valve output circuit. The board either cannot turn the valve on, cannot turn it off, or the valve is drawing the wrong current.

Causes include a failed gas valve solenoid, broken wire to the valve, or a damaged board MOSFET.
safetyWarning: Gas valve faults can lead to gas leakage. Do not bypass or jumper the valve.
symptoms: Inducer and igniter run but no flame

fixSteps.title: Check valve wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Verify both wires are firmly seated on the gas valve terminals.

fixSteps.title: Measure valve voltage
fixSteps.instruction: During trial for ignition, measure 24V at the valve. If present and valve does not open, replace valve.

whenToCallPro: Always call a pro for gas valve replacement — gas leak testing is required.

faq.q: Can a power outage cause a 7-flash?
faq.a: Rarely; persistent codes mean the valve or board is bad.

title: Low Flame Signal
shortDescription: Flame is lit but the sensor reads weak microamps.
fullDescription:
Eight flashes mean the burners ignite but the flame current is below threshold. The board allows operation but warns of an impending lockout.

The usual fix is to clean the flame sensor with fine emery cloth. White oxide buildup on the sensor rod blocks the rectified DC signal.

fixSteps.title: Clean flame sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Remove sensor and gently polish the rod with emery cloth or steel wool. Reinstall.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if cleaning does not restore signal above 1.5 microamps.

faq.q: How often should I clean the flame sensor?
faq.a: Once a year as part of annual maintenance.

title: Ignition Lockout
shortDescription: Furnace failed to light after three retry attempts.
fullDescription:
Nine flashes indicate a hard ignition lockout. The board attempted to ignite three times and failed, so it shut everything down for safety. The furnace will retry after one hour or after a power cycle.

Leading causes are a weak hot surface igniter, low gas pressure, or a closed manual gas shutoff.
safetyWarning: Confirm gas supply is on safely; do not search for gas leaks with an open flame.

fixSteps.title: Verify gas is on
fixSteps.instruction: Check the manual shutoff at the furnace and that other gas appliances work.

fixSteps.title: Test hot surface igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Power off and measure resistance — typically 40-200 ohms; open circuit means failed.

fixSteps.title: Replace igniter
fixSteps.instruction: Install a matching OEM or universal igniter. Avoid touching the silicon carbide element.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if igniter is good and gas pressure cannot be verified.

faq.q: How long do hot surface igniters last?
faq.a: Typically 4-7 years.

title: Normal Operation / No Call for Heat
shortDescription: Steady or slow continuous flash means board is healthy and waiting.
fullDescription:
A continuous slow flash on a Coleman furnace LED indicates the control board is powered, has no fault stored, and is waiting for a call for heat from the thermostat.

If the furnace will not start, the issue is upstream of the board: thermostat, transformer, or 24V wiring.

fixSteps.title: Check thermostat
fixSteps.instruction: Replace batteries and confirm setpoint is above room temperature.

fixSteps.title: Jumper R to W
fixSteps.instruction: Briefly jumper R and W terminals at the board; if furnace fires, problem is at thermostat or wiring.

whenToCallPro: Call a pro if 24V is missing at R-C with thermostat removed.

faq.a: No, it is the normal standby state.

title: Open high-limit
shortDescription: High-limit thermostat opened.
fullDescription: High-limit thermostat opened. Common diagnostic code on Coleman furnace. Resolve by following manufacturer service procedure for the implicated subsystem.

fixSteps.title: Power cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect power for 10 minutes, then restore.

fixSteps.title: Inspect
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the implicated component, wiring, and connectors.

fixSteps.title: Test/replace
fixSteps.instruction: Test sensor with multimeter or replace if reading abnormal.

fixSteps.title: Verify
fixSteps.instruction: Restore power, clear codes, run system to verify.

safetyWarning: Gas/electric appliance — turn off gas and disconnect electrical power before servicing.
whenToCallPro: Gas-appliance work usually requires licensed HVAC tech.

faq.a: Resolve before continued use to prevent damage or safety hazard.
Typically $200-$800 depending on the part.
